content.caption: Feature vs. Story Example
content.code:
# FEATURE (Program Level)

**Feature**: One-Click Checkout for Returning Users

**Description**:
As a returning customer,
I want to complete my purchase with a single click
So that I can check out faster and with less friction

**Benefits**:
- Reduce cart abandonment by 15%
- Improve customer satisfaction for repeat purchases
- Increase conversion rate for logged-in users

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- Returning users see "One-Click Checkout" button
- Payment method is automatically selected (last used)
- Order confirms within 2 seconds of click
- Works for all payment types (credit, PayPal)
- Security: requires user to be logged in

**Estimate**: 21 story points (total of all stories)

---

# STORIES (Team Level)

**Story 1 (Team A)**: One-Click Checkout UI
As a returning user,
I want to see a "One-Click Checkout" button on my cart
So that I know I can check out quickly

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- Button appears when user is logged in and has saved payment
- Button is prominently displayed above standard checkout
- Clicking button initiates checkout process
- Loading state shown during processing

**Estimate**: 5 points

---

**Story 2 (Team B)**: Secure Token Retrieval
As the system,
I want to securely retrieve the user's saved payment token
So that the one-click checkout can process payment

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- Token retrieved from secure storage
- Token decrypted correctly
- Fallback to standard checkout if token unavailable
- Logging for audit purposes

**Estimate**: 8 points

---

**Story 3 (Team A)**: Order Confirmation Flow
As a user using one-click checkout,
I want to see order confirmation immediately
So that I know my purchase was successful

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- Confirmation page loads within 2 seconds
- Order details displayed
- Email confirmation sent
- Analytics event fired

**Estimate**: 5 points

content.question: Scenario 2: A story is estimated at 13 points, which is too big for one iteration. What should happen?
options: Keep it as is—team can work on it across iterations
Split it into smaller stories that can each be completed in one iteration
content.explanation: In SAFe, stories should fit in one iteration. If a story is too big, it needs to be split into smaller, valuable stories. This enables continuous flow and accurate tracking. The same principle applies at feature level—features should fit in one PI.

content.title: Program Level - The Agile Release Train
The Agile Release Train (ART)
content.explanation:
The ART is the heart of SAFe. It's a long-lived, self-organizing team of Agile teams that plans, commits, and executes together.

**ART Characteristics**:
- 5-12 teams (50-125 people)
- All teams work toward a common mission
- Teams are cross-functional and self-organizing
- ART delivers value every Program Increment (PI)
- Typically 8-12 weeks per PI

**ART Roles**:

**Release Train Engineer (RTE)**
- Chief Scrum Master for the ART
- Facilitates PI Planning and ART events
- Coaches and mentors Scrum Masters
- Removes impediments at program level

**Product Management**
- Owns the Program Backlog
- Defines features and priorities
- Works with Product Owners on story breakdown
- Aligns with Portfolio on strategy

**System Architect/Engineering**
- Provides technical guidance
- Defines architectural direction
- Ensures technical consistency across teams

**Business Owners**
- Key stakeholders
- Provide business context
- Participate in PI Planning
- Evaluate feature completion

**Product Owners**
- Team-level backlog owners
- Part of PO sync for alignment

**Scrum Masters**
- Team coaches
- Participate in Scrum Master sync

**Development Teams**
- The people doing the work

**Customers and Stakeholders**
- Provide feedback at demos

content.title: Agile Release Train Structure
content.caption: The ART brings multiple teams together to deliver value in Program Increments

content.title: Program Increment (PI) Planning
content.explanation:
PI Planning is the heartbeat of the ART. It's a regular, face-to-face event where all ART members align on a shared mission and plan the next 8-12 weeks.

**PI Planning Basics**:
- 2-day event (in person ideally)
- Happens every 8-12 weeks
- All ART members attend (50-125 people)
- Results in committed PI objectives

**PI Planning Agenda**:

**Day 1 Morning**:
- Business context presentation (Product Management)
- Product vision and roadmap
- Architecture vision (System Architect)
- Team breakout #1: Teams draft their plans

**Day 1 Afternoon**:
- Team plan reviews (each team presents)
- Identify risks and dependencies
- Management reviews and adjusts

**Day 2 Morning**:
- Team breakout #2: Refine plans, address dependencies
- Integration of plans across teams

**Day 2 Afternoon**:
- Final plan review
- Risk review (ROAM: Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated)
- Confidence vote
- PI objectives finalized

**Confidence Vote**:
Teams vote on their confidence in the plan:
- Fist of five: 1 (no confidence) to 5 (very confident)
- Scores below 3 trigger discussion and replanning

**Outputs**:
- Committed PI objectives
- Program board showing dependencies
- Identified risks and ROAMed
- Social contracts renewed

content.title: PI Planning Flow
content: KEY INSIGHT: The magic happens in the breakout rooms—
teams talking to teams, solving dependencies together.
content.caption: PI Planning is a structured 2-day event that aligns the entire ART

content.title: ART Events and Cadence
content.explanation:
Beyond PI Planning, the ART has regular events to stay aligned:

**PI Execution** (8-12 weeks):
- Teams run their iterations (usually 4-5 iterations per PI)
- Each iteration includes standard Scrum events

**Iteration Sync** (weekly):
- Representatives from each team meet
- Discuss progress, dependencies, impediments
- Not a status report—a coordination meeting

**PO Sync** (weekly):
- Product Owners meet with Product Management
- Align on priorities, clarify features
- Prepare for next iteration

**Scrum Master Sync** (weekly):
- Scrum Masters meet with RTE
- Share impediments, solutions, improvements
- Cross-team coaching

**System Demo** (end of each iteration):
- Integrated demo of all teams' work
- Not just individual team demos
- Shows the entire system increment
- Stakeholders attend

**Inspect & Adapt Workshop** (last day of PI):
- Half-day event after final iteration
- Review PI performance against objectives
- Quantitative and qualitative review
- Problem-solving workshop
- Create improvement backlog for next PI

**PI Retrospective**:
- Teams reflect on PI process
- Identify systemic improvements
- Feed into next PI Planning

content.title: PI Planning Success
content.scenario: ART with 8 teams plans their first PI together
content.outcome: Teams identify and resolve 15 dependencies during planning
content.details: During PI Planning breakout, Team A realizes they need an API from Team B that wasn't planned. They negotiate: Team B will deliver the API in Iteration 2; Team A will build the UI in Iteration 3. They mark the dependency on the program board. Without PI Planning, this would have been discovered in Week 3, causing delays. Instead, it's solved before work starts.

content.question: Scenario 3: During PI Planning, a team presents their plan, and you see a critical dependency on another team that hasn't been discussed. What should happen?
options: Ignore it—teams will figure it out
Stop the presentation and have the two teams discuss immediately to resolve the dependency
content.explanation: PI Planning is the time to resolve dependencies. The RTE should facilitate a conversation between the two teams right then. They can negotiate timing, scope, or find alternatives. The goal is to leave planning with all dependencies addressed, not discovered later.

content.title: Lean Portfolio Management
content.explanation:
The Portfolio level aligns strategy with execution through Lean Portfolio Management (LPM).

**LPM Responsibilities**:

**Strategy and Investment Funding**:
- Establish strategic themes
- Define Lean budgets (not project budgets)
- Allocate funding to value streams
- Measure ROI and value delivery

**Program Portfolio Management**:
- Coordinate multiple ARTs
- Manage large epics through the Kanban system
- Ensure alignment with strategy

**Lean Governance**:
- Lightweight, decentralized decision-making
- Monitor key performance indicators
- Adjust based on feedback

**Portfolio Roles**:

**Epic Owners**:
- Steer epics from ideation to completion
- Coordinate with ARTs and Solution Trains
- Report on epic progress

**Enterprise Architect**:
- Define technical strategy
- Ensure architectural consistency
- Guide technology investments

**Lean Portfolio Management Team**:
- Senior leaders
- Make investment decisions
- Set strategic direction

content.title: Epics and the Portfolio Kanban
content.explanation:
Epics are large initiatives that span multiple PIs and often multiple ARTs. They're managed through a Portfolio Kanban system.

**Epic Kanban States**:

**1. Funnel**: All ideas captured
- No filtering yet
- Anyone can submit

**2. Review**: Initial evaluation
- Epic Owner reviews
- Assess fit with strategy
- Lightweight business case

**3. Analysis**: Deep dive
- Develop detailed business case
- Estimate cost and value
- Identify impacted ARTs

**4. Portfolio Backlog**: Approved and waiting
- Ready for implementation
- Prioritized against other epics

**5. Implementation**: Being executed
- Split into features
- Assigned to ARTs
- Progress tracked

**6. Done**: Completed
- Measured against business case
- Benefits realized

**Epic Hierarchy**:
- **Portfolio Epic**: Affects multiple ARTs, requires significant investment
- **Large Solution Epic**: Affects multiple Solution Trains (in Large Solution SAFe)
- **Program Epic**: Affects single ART, can be managed at Program level

**Epic Example**:
"Transform customer onboarding experience across all products" — would be a Portfolio Epic affecting multiple ARTs.

content.title: Portfolio Epic Kanban
content: │ Risks: Integration with legacy systems (mitigation plan in place)│
content.caption: The Portfolio Kanban manages epics from idea to done

content.title: Lean Budgeting
content.explanation:
Traditional project-based budgeting doesn't work with Agile. SAFe uses Lean Budgeting instead.

**Problems with Project Budgeting**:
- Funding ends when project ends (teams disband)
- Encourages starting many projects, finishing few
- Hard to adapt to changing priorities
- Creates competition for resources

**Lean Budgeting Principles**:

**Fund Value Streams, Not Projects**:
- Allocate budget to long-lived value streams
- Teams stay together
- Continuous funding, not start/stop

**Establish Guardrails**:
- Define spending limits
- Set approval thresholds
- Allow decentralized decisions within boundaries

**Use Participatory Budgeting**:
- Stakeholders allocate funds to initiatives
- Creates shared ownership
- Faster decisions

**Measure Outcomes, Not Output**:
- Track value delivered, not budget spent
- Adjust based on results

**Budget Tiers**:
1. **Run the Business**: Ongoing operations, maintenance
2. **Grow the Business**: Enhancements, new features
3. **Transform the Business**: Strategic initiatives, innovation

**Lean Budgeting in Action**:
Instead of approving a 6-month, $1M project, LPM allocates $4M annually to the "Customer Experience" value stream. The ART decides how to spend it across features, with governance through epic approval process. If priorities shift, they reallocate within the value stream without asking permission.

content.title: Lean Budgeting Success
content.scenario: Company shifts from project to Lean budgeting
content.outcome: 50% less time spent on budgeting, more value delivered
content.prevention: No more projects dying when funding runs out
content.details: Before: Annual budgeting process took 3 months. Each project had separate funding. Teams formed and disbanded. Projects frequently ran out of money before delivering value. After: Funded 5 value streams with annual budgets. Teams stable. Decisions made at value stream level within guardrails. Epic approval takes days, not months. Value delivery increased 40%. Team morale improved.

content.question: Scenario 4: A company funds projects annually. Teams form, deliver a project, then disband. What SAFe principle would help?
options: Switch to Lean Budgeting—fund value streams, keep teams stable
content.explanation: Project-based funding creates unstable teams, handoffs, and waste. Lean Budgeting funds long-lived value streams with stable teams. Teams stay together, build domain knowledge, and continuously improve. This is a fundamental shift in how to think about investment.

content.title: The SAFe Implementation Roadmap
content.explanation:
SAFe provides a proven implementation roadmap:

**1. Reaching the Tipping Point**
- Identify champions and leaders
- Build urgency for change
- Assess current state

**2. Train Lean-Agile Change Agents**
- Train internal coaches
- Get SPC (SAFe Program Consultant) certified
- Build capability

**3. Train Executives and Leaders**
- Leading SAFe training
- Leaders understand their role
- Commitment to change

**4. Identify Value Streams and ARTs**
- Map value streams
- Identify first ART
- Define ART boundaries

**5. Create the Implementation Plan**
- PI Planning dates
- Training plan
- Metrics and milestones

**6. Launch First ART**
- Train teams (SAFe for Teams)
- PI Planning event
- Execute first PI

**7. Coach ART Execution**
- Support teams
- Facilitate events
- Remove impediments

**8. Launch More ARTs**
- Repeat for additional value streams
- Scale incrementally

**9. Extend to Portfolio**
- Add Portfolio level
- Implement Lean Budgeting
- Epic Kanban

**10. Sustain and Improve**
- Communities of practice
- Inspect & Adapt
- Continuous improvement

content.title: SAFe Implementation Roadmap
content: │  │ 1. Reaching Tipping Point ──▶ 2. Train Change Agents      │  │
KEY INSIGHT: Implement incrementally. Don't try to do everything
at once. Start with one ART, learn, then expand.
content.caption: The SAFe Implementation Roadmap provides a proven path to adoption

content.title: SAFe Certifications
content.explanation:
SAFe offers a comprehensive certification path for different roles:

**For Team Members**:
- SAFe for Teams (SP)
- SAFe Scrum Master (SSM)
- SAFe Product Owner/Product Manager (POPM)

**For Program Level**:
- SAFe Release Train Engineer (RTE)
- SAFe Advanced Scrum Master (SASM)
- SAFe Product Manager (PM)

**For Portfolio Level**:
- SAFe Lean Portfolio Management (LPM)
- SAFe Agile Product Management (APM)

**For Architects**:
- SAFe Architect (ARCH)

**For Coaches and Implementers**:
- SAFe Program Consultant (SPC)
- SAFe Practice Consultant (SPC)

**Certification Paths**:
- Most certifications require attending a course
- Many require passing an exam
- Renewal required annually

**Value of Certification**:
- Common language across organization
- Proven knowledge base
- Access to community and resources
- Credibility for coaches

**But**: Certification alone doesn't make someone a great practitioner. Experience and mindset matter more.

content.title: SAFe Success Factors and Common Pitfalls
content.explanation:
What makes SAFe succeed—and what causes it to fail?

**Success Factors**:

**Leadership Commitment**:
- Leaders actively participate
- They change their own behaviors
- They remove impediments

**Start Small, Learn, Expand**:
- First ART is critical
- Don't try to implement everything at once
- Learn from early mistakes

**Invest in Training**:
- Everyone understands the framework
- Common language and practices
- Certified coaches guide the way

**Focus on Culture, Not Just Process**:
- SAFe is a means, not an end
- Build trust, transparency, continuous improvement
- Leaders model desired behaviors

**Measure What Matters**:
- Track outcomes, not just outputs
- Use metrics to improve, not judge
- Adjust based on data

**Common Pitfalls**:

**SAFe-But**:
- "We do SAFe, but not PI Planning" (then you don't do SAFe)
- Cherry-picking practices without the structure

**Mechanical Implementation**:
- Doing the ceremonies without the spirit
- Zombie SAFe—going through motions

**Top-Down Forcing**:
- Mandating SAFe without buy-in
- Teams resist, culture suffers

**Underinvesting in Coaching**:
- No internal coaches
- Teams flounder

**Not Adapting SAFe**:
- Applying SAFe rigidly without considering context
- SAFe is a framework—adapt it

**Ignoring Technical Practices**:
- Focusing only on process, not engineering excellence
- Built-in quality requires technical discipline

content.title: SAFe Transformation Success
content.scenario: Large financial services company transforms with SAFe
content.outcome: 50% faster time to market, 30% higher employee engagement
content.prevention: Avoided common pitfalls through phased approach
content.details: Company with 2000 IT staff, traditional waterfall. Started with pilot ART of 7 teams. Trained everyone. Did first PI Planning—chaotic but valuable. Coached heavily. First PI delivered value. Expanded to 3 more ARTs. Added Portfolio level after 18 months. Key success factors: CEO attended first PI Planning, leaders changed behavior, invested in 10 internal coaches, celebrated early wins. After 3 years, transformation complete. Now 20 ARTs, continuous delivery, market leader.

content.question: Scenario 5: A company decides to 'do SAFe' by training everyone, buying the tools, and mandating all teams use it. Six months later, nothing has improved. What's likely missing?
options: They implemented mechanically without culture change, coaching, and leadership commitment
content.explanation: This is classic 'mechanical implementation.' SAFe requires culture change, active leadership, and ongoing coaching. Mandating practices without changing mindset leads to 'zombie SAFe'—ceremonies without value. The missing pieces: leaders modeling change, internal coaches, focus on continuous improvement, and adapting SAFe to context.

content.value:
Remember: SAFe is a framework, not a prescription. It provides proven patterns for scaling Agile, but it must be adapted to your context. The goal isn't to 'do SAFe'—it's to achieve business agility. SAFe is just a means to that end.

Start small. Learn fast. Celebrate wins. Adapt constantly. And never forget that at the heart of SAFe are people—teams building great products, leaders enabling their success, and customers receiving value faster.

When SAFe is done well, it's not bureaucracy—it's a well-orchestrated system delivering value at scale. When it's done poorly, it's just more meetings. Your job is to ensure the former.

tutorials.title: 🔄 LeSS Framework - Large-Scale Scrum Done Right
tutorials.description: Master Large-Scale Scrum (LeSS) for scaling Agile with minimal added process. Learn how LeSS applies Scrum principles to multiple teams working on one product, preserving simplicity while enabling coordination.

content.title: The Heart of LeSS - Scrum Scaled, Not Invented
What is LeSS?
content.explanation:
LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) is a framework for scaling Scrum to multiple teams working on one product. Unlike other scaling frameworks that add new roles, artifacts, and processes, LeSS starts with standard Scrum and asks: 'How can we scale this with as little added complexity as possible?'

**The LeSS Philosophy**:
More than 90% of scaling is about simplifying the organization, not adding complexity. LeSS removes organizational complexity rather than adding framework complexity.

**LeSS Principles**:

**1. Large-Scale Scrum is Still Scrum**:
- One Product Owner
- One Product Backlog
- One Definition of Done
- One shippable product increment each sprint

**2. Empirical Process Control**:
- Transparency, inspection, adaptation at all levels
- Teams learn and adjust together

**3. Systems Thinking**:
- Optimize the whole, not parts
- Local optimization is global suboptimization

**4. Customer-Centric**:
- Deliver value to customers frequently
- Short feedback loops

**5. Continuous Improvement**:
- Kaizen at scale
- Everyone improves the system

**Key Insight**: LeSS is Scrum, just with multiple teams. It adds no new roles, no new artifacts, and minimal new events. Complexity is handled through simplicity.

content.title: LeSS vs. Traditional Scaling
content: │  │ Portfolio Manager, Epic Owners, Lean Governance...        │  │
│  │ Program Manager, Release Train Engineer, PI Planning...   │  │
│  │ Scrum Masters, Product Owners, Development Teams...       │  │
LeSS SCALING: Scrum with Multiple Teams
│  One Product Owner, One Product Backlog                         │
│  One Definition of Done, One Shippable Product                 │
│  │ Scrum Team │ │ Scrum Team │ │ Scrum Team │ │ Scrum Team │   │
│  │ • PO part  │ │ • PO part  │ │ • PO part  │ │ • PO part  │   │
│  │ • SM part  │ │ • SM part  │ │ • SM part  │ │ • SM part  │   │
KEY INSIGHT: LeSS adds events, not layers. The structure
remains flat, roles remain the same.
content.caption: LeSS scales by adding events, not layers of management

content.title: LeSS vs. LeSS Huge
content.explanation:
LeSS comes in two flavors: LeSS (for up to 8 teams) and LeSS Huge (for more than 8 teams).

**LeSS (Basic)**:
- 2-8 teams (up to ~80 people)
- One Product Owner
- One Product Backlog
- All teams work on the same product
- One sprint, one shippable increment
- Simple rules, minimal added structure

**LeSS Huge**:
- 8+ teams (hundreds of people)
- Multiple teams organized by feature areas called 'Requirement Areas'
- Area Product Owners (APOs) for each area
- One overall Product Owner
- One product, one backlog, but with area backlogs
- More coordination, but still minimal framework

**When to Use Which**:
- Start with LeSS for up to 8 teams
- If you grow beyond, consider LeSS Huge
- Don't start with LeSS Huge—scale gradually

**The 8-Team Threshold**:
Research suggests that 8 teams (about 80 people) is the maximum that can effectively coordinate with simple LeSS. Beyond that, you need some structure—hence LeSS Huge.

content.title: LeSS Principles in Depth
content.explanation:
LeSS is guided by ten principles that shape every practice:

**1. Large-Scale Scrum is Still Scrum**
No new roles, no new artifacts. Just Scrum with multiple teams.

**2. Empirical Process Control**
Transparency, inspection, adaptation. At scale, this means everyone sees everything.

**3. Systems Thinking**
Optimize the whole product, not individual teams. Local optimizations are global suboptimizations.

**4. Lean Thinking**
Eliminate waste, amplify learning, decide as late as possible, deliver fast.

**5. Customer-Centric**
Everyone understands customers. Short feedback loops. Deliver value frequently.

**6. Continuous Improvement**
Everyone improves the system. Retrospectives lead to experiments.

**7. Queuing Theory**
Limit work in progress. Reduce batch sizes. Manage queue lengths.

**8. Focus on the Whole Product**
Feature teams, not component teams. Everyone can work on any area.

**9. Management is Leadership**
Managers focus on improving the system, not controlling people.

**10. Organizational Design**
Structure follows product. Organize around value, not functions.

**These principles lead to concrete practices**:
- Feature teams over component teams
- One Product Backlog
- One Definition of Done across all teams
- Sprint reviews with all teams and stakeholders
- Cross-team coordination via informal communication, not added roles

content.question: Scenario 1: A company scaling to 4 teams wants to 'do LeSS.' They're considering adding a 'Program Manager' role to coordinate teams. What would LeSS say?
options: No new roles—teams coordinate directly. Add events, not layers.
Add the role but call it something else
content.explanation: LeSS adds no new roles. Coordination happens through events (Overall Sprint Planning, Overall Review) and direct team communication. Adding a Program Manager creates a layer of hierarchy, reducing team autonomy and adding complexity. Scale events, not management.

items.myth: LeSS is just Scrum with more teams
items.reality: It's exactly that—and that's the point. It adds no unnecessary complexity.

items.myth: LeSS doesn't scale to large organizations
items.reality: LeSS Huge handles hundreds of people on one product

items.myth: LeSS requires fewer meetings
items.reality: It adds some cross-team events, but removes layers of management overhead

items.myth: LeSS is only for co-located teams
items.reality: Works with distributed teams, though co-location helps

items.myth: LeSS is just an alternative to SAFe
items.reality: It's a different philosophy—minimalist vs. comprehensive

content.title: The Product Owner in LeSS
content.explanation:
In LeSS, there's still one Product Owner—even with multiple teams. This is non-negotiable.

**The Single Product Owner**:
- One person with final authority over the Product Backlog
- Responsible for maximizing value of the whole product
- Works with all teams, not just one
- Cannot delegate priority decisions

**How One PO Manages Multiple Teams**:

**1. Clear Prioritization**:
- The Product Backlog is single and ordered
- Teams pull work from the top
- No team backlogs—just one product backlog

**2. Area Product Owners (LeSS Huge)**:
- In LeSS Huge, Area POs support the overall PO
- They manage area backlogs within the overall priorities
- Still one overall PO with final authority

**3. PO Syncs with Teams**:
- Participates in Overall Sprint Planning
- Available for team questions
- Attends Sprint Reviews

**4. PO Works with Stakeholders**:
- Gathers input from all stakeholders
- Manages expectations
- Communicates priorities and trade-offs

**The PO's Time**:
- With multiple teams, the PO is full-time (often more)
- Cannot be part-time or shared across products
- Needs deep product and customer knowledge

**Key Principle**: One product, one backlog, one PO. Splitting the PO role splits the product vision.

content.title: The Scrum Master in LeSS
content.explanation:
LeSS also maintains the Scrum Master role, but with a broader focus.

**Scrum Master Responsibilities**:

**To Their Team**:
- Coaching on Scrum and Agile practices
- Removing impediments
- Facilitating team events
- Protecting the team

**Across Teams**:
- Coaching other teams when needed
- Facilitating cross-team coordination
- Helping with Overall Retrospective
- Identifying systemic impediments

**To the Organization**:
- Coaching management on Agile
- Helping with organizational change
- Removing organizational impediments

**Scrum Master Allocation**:
- In LeSS, Scrum Masters are typically dedicated
- One Scrum Master can serve 1-3 teams
- Focus is on coaching, not administration
- Scrum Masters are not team secretaries

**Scrum Master Community**:
- Scrum Masters meet regularly
- Share insights and challenges
- Improve coaching practices
- Work on systemic improvements

**Scrum Master vs. Team Lead**:
- Not a manager
- No authority over team members
- Serves the team, not the other way around

content.title: The Development Team in LeSS
content.explanation:
Development Teams in LeSS are feature teams, not component teams. This is crucial.

**Feature Teams vs. Component Teams**:

**Component Teams**:
- Own a technical component (database, UI, API)
- Work passes from team to team
- Handoffs, delays, integration hell
- Optimize locally, suboptimize globally

**Feature Teams**:
- Own end-to-end customer features
- Can work on any part of the codebase
- No handoffs—team delivers complete value
- Optimize for overall product

**Why Feature Teams Matter**:
- Reduce dependencies between teams
- Faster delivery (no waiting for other teams)
- Higher quality (end-to-end ownership)
- More motivation (see complete features)
- Easier planning (fewer cross-team dependencies)

**Making Feature Teams Work**:

**1. Cross-Functional Skills**:
- Teams need all skills (UI, backend, DB, testing)
- Invest in T-shaped people
- Learning is continuous

**2. Codebase Must Support It**:
- Modular architecture
- Clean separation of concerns
- Good test coverage for refactoring

**3. Teams Learn the Whole System**:
- Pairing across areas
- Mob programming
- Code rotation

**4. Management Supports Learning**:
- Time for learning
- Tolerance for initial slower velocity
- Focus on long-term gains

**Team Size**:
- Same as Scrum: 5-9 people
- Teams are stable, long-lived
- New members join, but teams persist

content.title: Component Teams vs. Feature Teams
content: COMPONENT TEAMS: Work Passes Between Teams
• Blame culture ("UI team did it wrong")
FEATURE TEAMS: Each Team Delivers End-to-End
content.caption: Feature teams eliminate handoffs and enable true end-to-end ownership

content.title: Transition to Feature Teams
content.scenario: Company with UI, backend, and database teams shifts to feature teams
content.outcome: Delivery time drops from 6 weeks to 1 week
content.prevention: No more handoffs, no more integration delays
content.details: Before: New feature required UI team (2 weeks), then backend team (2 weeks), then database team (1 week), then testing (1 week). Total 6 weeks, plus integration hell. After: Three feature teams, each with UI, backend, database, and testing skills. A feature is picked up by one team and delivered in 1 week. No handoffs, no waiting. Teams happier, customers happier. Initial learning curve, but massive long-term gains.

content.question: Scenario 2: A LeSS implementation has teams organized by technical layer (UI, backend, database). What problem will they likely face?
options: High dependency, handoffs, and slow delivery
This is how LeSS recommends organizing
content.explanation: Component teams create handoffs and dependencies. LeSS recommends feature teams that can deliver end-to-end value. The component team structure will likely lead to slow delivery, integration problems, and low morale. Transitioning to feature teams is a key LeSS practice.

content.title: Overall Sprint Planning
content.explanation:
With multiple teams, Sprint Planning has two parts: Overall and Team.

**Overall Sprint Planning (Part 1)**:

**Who Attends**:
- Product Owner
- All teams (representatives or everyone)
- Scrum Masters (optional)

**Duration**: 1-2 hours (for 2-4 teams) to half-day (for more)

**Agenda**:
1. **PO presents top of backlog**: Highest priority items for the sprint
2. **Teams discuss**: Which team will work on what? How will they coordinate?
3. **Clarify requirements**: Teams ask questions, PO clarifies
4. **Identify dependencies**: Teams note cross-team dependencies
5. **Draft team assignments**: Tentative which team takes which items

**Outcome**:
- Clear which items each team will likely take
- Identified dependencies
- Shared understanding of sprint goal

**Team Sprint Planning (Part 2)**:
- Each team plans its own work in detail
- Breaks items into tasks
- Creates team sprint backlog
- Estimates within the team

**Key Points**:
- Overall planning is collaborative, not top-down
- Teams self-select work (PO doesn't assign)
- Dependencies are surfaced and managed
- Multiple teams can work on same feature

content.title: Overall Sprint Review
content.explanation:
The Sprint Review is done together, with all teams and stakeholders.

**Why Together?**:
- Show the integrated product, not just team parts
- Stakeholders see the whole picture
- Cross-team feedback
- Build shared ownership

**Format Options**:

**Option A: Demo Fair**
- Each team has a station
- Stakeholders walk around, see demos, ask questions
- Informal, interactive
- Good for many teams

**Option B: Plenary with Breakouts**
- All together for intro and wrap-up
- Teams demo in parallel sessions
- Stakeholders choose what to see

**Option C: Sequential Demos**
- Each team demos for 5-10 minutes
- All stakeholders see everything
- Can be long with many teams

**What's Demoed**:
- Working, tested software
- Integrated across teams where possible
- Real features, not prototypes

**Who Attends**:
- All teams (or representatives)
- Product Owner
- Stakeholders (customers, users, management)
- Scrum Masters

**Agenda (2-hour example)**:
- 0:00 - Welcome and context (PO)
- 0:10 - Demo session (fair or breakouts)
- 1:30 - Feedback gathering
- 1:45 - Review of timeline, budget, progress
- 1:55 - Close and next steps

**Outcome**:
- Stakeholder feedback on the product
- Updated backlog based on feedback
- Shared understanding of progress

content.title: Overall Sprint Review Formats
content: │  Pros: Interactive, flexible, many demos at once               │
│  Cons: Stakeholders may miss some demos                         │
│  │ Room A:  │  │ Room B:  │  │ Room C:  │                      │
│  Cons: Can be long and passive for large groups                │
content.caption: Choose the review format that works best for your context and number of teams

content.title: Overall Retrospective
content.explanation:
The Overall Retrospective focuses on the whole system, not individual teams.

**Purpose**:
- Improve how teams work together
- Identify systemic impediments
- Improve the development process across teams
- Strengthen collaboration

**Who Attends**:
- Representatives from each team (2-3 people)
- Product Owner
- Scrum Masters
- Managers (if invited, as listeners)

**Frequency**:
- After each sprint (or every 2-3 sprints)
- More frequent when problems arise
- At least once per release

**Agenda (2-3 hours)**:

**1. Set the Stage (15 min)**
- Review agenda and goals
- Safety check-in

**2. Gather Data (30 min)**
- What worked well across teams?
- What problems did we face?
- Review cross-team metrics

**3. Generate Insights (45 min)**
- Identify root causes of systemic issues
- Use techniques like 5 Whys, fishbone
- Prioritize areas to improve

**4. Decide What to Do (30 min)**
- Choose 1-3 experiments
- Define actions and owners
- Set checkpoints

**5. Close (15 min)**
- Review decisions
- Thank participants

**Themes Often Emerge**:
- Dependency management
- Integration challenges
- Communication gaps
- Shared technical practices
- Architecture issues

**Follow-up**:
- Experiments tried in next sprint
- Reviewed at next Overall Retro
- Systemic changes escalated to management

content.title: The Product Backlog in LeSS
content.explanation:
LeSS maintains a single Product Backlog for the whole product—even with many teams.

**Characteristics**:

**Single, Ordered Backlog**:
- One list for all teams
- Ordered by value, risk, dependencies
- Top items are small and clear
- Lower items may be larger

**Items Are Customer-Focused**:
- Features, not technical tasks
- Expressed in customer language
- Clear acceptance criteria

**No Team Backlogs**:
- Teams don't have separate backlogs
- They pull from the common backlog
- Prevents local optimization

**Backlog Refinement**:
- Done regularly with all teams
- PO presents upcoming items
- Teams ask questions, give estimates
- Items get split and clarified

**Size of Items**:
- Top: small (fit in one sprint)
- Middle: larger (will be split)
- Bottom: epics, ideas

**Estimates**:
- Teams estimate together
- Relative sizing (story points)
- Teams may have different velocities
- Use historical data for forecasting

**The PO's Role**:
- Owns the backlog
- Makes priority decisions
- Explains value and context
- Incorporates stakeholder feedback

content.title: Overall Retrospective Success
content.scenario: Teams struggling with integration issues each sprint
content.outcome: Systemic fix reduces integration time 80%
content.prevention: Problem solved at root, not band-aided
content.details: Overall Retrospective: Teams report spending 2 days each sprint on integration. Data gathering shows main issue: teams working on same code areas without coordination. Root cause: architecture leads to frequent conflicts. Solution: Architecture team refactors to create clearer boundaries. Teams also start daily integration sync. Integration time drops to 2 hours. Problem solved systemically, not by blaming teams.

content.question: Scenario 3: Teams in a LeSS implementation keep having integration problems at the end of sprints. Where should this be discussed?
content.explanation: Integration problems across multiple teams are systemic, not team-specific. The Overall Retrospective is designed to identify and address such cross-team issues. Individual team retros might discuss symptoms, but the root cause needs systemic discussion.

content.title: LeSS Adoption Steps
content.explanation:
Adopting LeSS is organizational change, not just process change. Here's a typical path:

**Step 1: Education**
- Leaders attend LeSS training
- Teams learn LeSS basics
- Everyone understands principles

**Step 2: Start with One Product**
- Choose a product (not a project)
- Identify initial teams (2-4)
- Keep other teams stable

**Step 3: Form Feature Teams**
- Reorganize into cross-functional feature teams
- This is hard—invest in it
- Expect temporary slowdown

**Step 4: First Sprint**
- Use LeSS events: Overall Planning, Team Planning, etc.
- One Product Backlog
- One Definition of Done
- Deliver integrated increment

**Step 5: Learn and Adapt**
- Overall Retrospective after first sprint
- Identify what's working, what's not
- Adjust, experiment

**Step 6: Expand**
- Add more teams
- Improve architecture
- Deepen technical practices
- Scale to more products

**Common Challenges**:

**Challenge 1: Component Team Legacy**
Moving to feature teams is hard. People have specialized skills and identities.
- *Solution*: Pairing, mob programming, learning budget

**Challenge 2: Manager Resistance**
Managers fear losing power or purpose.
- *Solution*: Educate on new management role (improving system)

**Challenge 3: Architecture Constraints**
Codebase may not support feature teams.
- *Solution*: Refactor, modularize, invest in architecture

**Challenge 4: One PO Capacity**
One PO may be overwhelmed.
- *Solution*: Strong PO, supported by teams, clear backlog

content.title: LeSS Adoption Journey
content: KEY INSIGHT: Adoption takes 1-3 years. Be patient,
but persistent. Celebrate small wins along the way.
content.caption: LeSS adoption is a multi-year journey of organizational change

content.title: Management in LeSS
content.explanation:
Management's role changes dramatically in LeSS. They're not command-and-control; they're system designers.

**Traditional Management**:
- Assign work to people
- Monitor progress
- Solve problems for teams
- Make decisions
- Control outcomes

**LeSS Management**:
- Design the organization
- Improve the system
- Remove impediments
- Coach and teach
- Focus on long-term improvement

**Management Responsibilities**:

**1. Organizational Design**:
- Structure around value, not functions
- Create feature teams
- Ensure teams have needed skills

**2. Goal Setting**:
- Set vision and direction
- Define outcomes, not outputs
- Align with strategy

**3. Capability Development**:
- Invest in training and coaching
- Support learning
- Build T-shaped skills

**4. Remove Impediments**:
- Identify systemic blockers
- Change policies that hinder agility
- Provide resources

**5. Lead by Example**:
- Model desired behaviors
- Be transparent
- Show vulnerability

**Management Chains**:
- Fewer layers
- Focus on value streams
- Managers as teachers

**The Manager's Question**:
Not "Are teams delivering?" but "How can I improve the system so teams can deliver better?"

content.title: LeSS and Technical Practices
content.explanation:
LeSS emphasizes technical excellence as essential for scaling. Without it, scaling fails.

**Why Technical Practices Matter**:
- Feature teams need to work anywhere in codebase
- Multiple teams modify same code
- Integration must be continuous
- Quality must be built in

**Essential Technical Practices**:

**Continuous Integration (CI)**:
- All code integrated daily (hourly)
- Automated builds and tests
- Fast feedback

**Test Automation**:
- Unit tests
- Integration tests
- Acceptance tests
- Run with every build

**Test-Driven Development (TDD)**:
- Tests before code
- Clean, testable design
- Regression safety

**Refactoring**:
- Improve code structure
- Reduce technical debt
- Enable feature teams

**Collective Code Ownership**:
- Anyone can change any code
- No code silos
- Shared responsibility

**Simple Design**:
- Just enough design
- Evolve architecture
- Avoid over-engineering

**Pair/Mob Programming**:
- Share knowledge
- Improve quality
- Cross-train

**Continuous Delivery**:
- Deploy frequently
- Reduce release risk
- Get feedback faster

**The Technical Debt Trap**:
Without these practices, feature teams get slower. Code becomes harder to change. Coordination becomes painful. LeSS implementation stalls.

**Invest Early**:
Don't wait to improve technical practices. Start day one. Make time for refactoring. Invest in automation. The payoff is exponential.

content.title: Technical Practices Enable LeSS
content.scenario: Company adopts LeSS but ignores technical practices
content.outcome: Teams struggle, velocity drops, morale falls
content.prevention: After investing in TDD and CI, they turn around
content.details: Company formed feature teams and started LeSS. But codebase was messy, tests were slow, integration was painful. Teams spent 30% of time merging code. Velocity dropped 40%. Leadership invested 3 months in technical improvement: TDD training, CI pipeline upgrade, refactoring sprints. After 6 months, velocity recovered and exceeded previous levels. Teams now work in any part of codebase confidently. LeSS now working.

content.question: Scenario 4: A LeSS implementation is struggling. Teams report constant merge conflicts and slow builds. What's the likely root cause?
options: Inadequate technical practices (CI, test automation, refactoring)
content.explanation: Merge conflicts and slow builds are technical issues. Multiple teams can't work effectively on one codebase without strong technical practices: continuous integration, test automation, and clean architecture. The solution is to invest in technical excellence, not more meetings.

content.title: LeSS Community and Resources
content.explanation:
LeSS has a vibrant community and rich resources for learning.

**Key Resources**:

**Books**:
- "Large-Scale Scrum: More with LeSS" by Craig Larman and Bas Vodde
- "Practices for Scaling Lean & Agile Development" also by Larman & Vodde

**Website**: less.works
- Case studies
- Articles
- Framework descriptions

**Training and Certification**:
- LeSS Practitioner (3-day course)
- LeSS for Executives
- LeSS Scrum Master

**Community**:
- LeSS meetups worldwide
- Online discussion groups
- Annual LeSS conferences

**Case Studies**:
- Real-world implementations
- Lessons learned
- Available on less.works

**Open Source**:
- Many LeSS materials are freely available
- Framework is open and transparent

**Getting Started**:
- Read the book
- Take a course
- Join community discussions
- Start small with one product
- Learn from others' mistakes

**The LeSS Mindset**:
LeSS is more than a framework—it's a philosophy. It values simplicity, systems thinking, and continuous improvement. The community embodies these values.

content.value:
Remember: LeSS is Scrum. Not Scrum with add-ons, not Scrum modified—just Scrum applied to multiple teams working on one product.

The magic is in what LeSS removes: layers of management, complex coordination roles, separate backlogs, component silos. By removing complexity, LeSS enables teams to focus on what matters: delivering value.

LeSS is hard because it requires real organizational change. It's easy because it doesn't invent new complexity. It just asks you to apply Scrum principles honestly at scale.

When LeSS works, it's beautiful: multiple teams, one product, one rhythm, one goal. No handoffs, no delays, no blame. Just teams building great software together.

tutorials.title: 🔗 Nexus Framework - Scaling Scrum with Minimalism
tutorials.description: Master the Nexus framework for scaling Scrum to 3-9 teams. Learn how Nexus adds just enough structure to coordinate multiple teams while preserving Scrum's simplicity and empiricism.

content.title: The Heart of Nexus - Scrum Scaled, Not Replaced
What is the Nexus Framework?
content.explanation:
Nexus is a framework for scaling Scrum to multiple teams working on a single product. Developed by Ken Schwaber (co-creator of Scrum) and Scrum.org, Nexus adds minimal structure to coordinate up to 9 teams (approximately 3-9 teams, or 30-90 people).

**The Core Idea**:
Nexus extends Scrum by adding a thin layer of integration and coordination—just enough to handle the complexity of multiple teams, while preserving Scrum's principles and practices.

**Nexus is NOT**:
- A new framework (it's Scrum plus integration)
- A replacement for Scrum (it includes Scrum)
- A set of new roles (it adds one new role)
- Bureaucracy (it adds minimal events)

**Key Principles**:

**1. One Product Backlog**:
All teams work from a single, prioritized backlog.

**2. One Definition of Done**:
All teams share the same quality standards.

**3. One Integrated Increment**:
At least once per sprint, teams integrate their work into a whole.

**4. Transparency**:
Cross-team dependencies and issues are visible.

**5. Accountability**:
One Nexus Integration Team is accountable for the integrated increment.

**Key Insight**: Nexus doesn't invent new ways of working—it creates a container for multiple Scrum teams to work together effectively.

content.title: Nexus Framework Overview
content: │  │ • Nexus Integration Team members (usually 1-2 per team)   │  │
│  │  │ Scrum Team │ │ Scrum Team │ │ Scrum Team │           │  │
│ • Nexus Sprint Backlog (overview of team backlogs)             │
│ • Integrated Increment (at least once per sprint)              │
│ • Nexus Goal (overall sprint goal for all teams)               │
content.caption: Nexus adds an integration layer above Scrum teams

content.title: When to Use Nexus
content.explanation:
Nexus is designed for a specific context: multiple Scrum teams working on the same product.

**Ideal for Nexus**:
- 3-9 teams (approx 30-90 people)
- One product, one backlog
- Teams need to integrate frequently
- Dependencies exist between teams
- Organization already does Scrum well

**Not Ideal for Nexus**:
- Single team (use Scrum)
- 10+ teams (consider LeSS Huge or SAFe)
- Multiple unrelated products
- Teams that don't need to integrate
- Organizations not doing Scrum well yet

**Signs You Need Nexus**:
- Dependencies between teams cause delays
- Integration is painful and happens at end
- Multiple teams affect same code areas
- "It works on my machine" across teams
- Sprint reviews show parts, not whole
- Hard to see overall progress

**Nexus vs. Other Scaling Frameworks**:

| Aspect | Nexus | LeSS | SAFe |
|--------|-------|------|------|
| Team count | 3-9 | Up to 8 (LeSS), 8+ (LeSS Huge) | Any (with ARTs) |
| New roles | 1 (NIT members) | None (LeSS), Area POs (Huge) | Many |
| New events | 4 (Nexus events) | Overall events | PI Planning, many |
| Complexity | Low | Low | Medium-High |
| Philosophy | Minimal addition | Pure Scrum | Comprehensive |

**Key Insight**: Choose Nexus when you want to scale Scrum with minimal added complexity—just enough to handle integration.

content.question: Scenario 1: A company has 5 teams working on the same product. They're using Scrum well, but integration is a nightmare—teams integrate at the end of sprints and it always breaks. What should they consider?
options: Keep doing what they're doing—integration is always hard
Nexus—it's designed for exactly this problem
content.explanation: This is the classic problem Nexus solves. Teams are doing Scrum well but struggling with cross-team integration. Nexus adds just enough structure (Nexus Integration Team, Nexus events) to ensure integration happens throughout the sprint, not at the end.

items.myth: Nexus is just Scrum with more meetings
items.reality: Nexus adds specific integration events, not just more meetings

items.myth: You need special software for Nexus
items.reality: Same Scrum tools work—just coordinate across teams

items.myth: Nexus replaces Scrum
items.reality: Nexus includes Scrum; teams still do all Scrum events

items.myth: Nexus only works for co-located teams
items.reality: Works for distributed teams with good communication practices

items.myth: Nexus is less powerful than other frameworks
items.reality: It's intentionally minimal—power comes from simplicity

content.title: The Nexus Integration Team
content.explanation:
The Nexus Integration Team (NIT) is the only new role in Nexus. It's accountable for ensuring the integrated increment is produced at least once per sprint.

**NIT Composition**:
- **Product Owner** (overall PO for the product)
- **Scrum Master** (facilitates Nexus events)
- **Nexus Integration Team Members** (usually 1-2 representatives from each Scrum Team)

**NIT Responsibilities**:

**1. Coordinate and Coach**:
- Help teams integrate their work
- Coach teams on cross-team collaboration
- Remove cross-team impediments

**2. Ensure Integration**:
- Define integration strategy
- Ensure integrated increment meets DoD
- Manage dependencies

**3. Manage the Nexus Backlog**:
- Refine the overall Product Backlog
- Identify cross-team dependencies
- Ensure backlog items are appropriately sized

**4. Facilitate Nexus Events**:
- Nexus Sprint Planning
- Nexus Daily Scrum
- Nexus Sprint Review
- Nexus Retrospective

**5. Report Progress**:
- Track overall progress toward Nexus Goal
- Communicate with stakeholders
- Escalate systemic issues

**NIT Members**:
- Not a separate role—existing team members
- Spend part of their time on NIT duties
- Bring team perspective to integration
- Take integration knowledge back to teams

**Key Point**: The NIT doesn't do the integration work—teams do. The NIT ensures integration happens.

content.title: Product Owner in Nexus
content.explanation:
The Product Owner role in Nexus is similar to Scrum, but with broader scope.

**One Product Owner**:
- Single PO for the whole product
- Accountable for value across all teams
- Works with all teams, not just one

**Responsibilities**:

**1. Manage the Product Backlog**:
- Single, prioritized backlog for all teams
- Items clear and ready for multiple teams
- Dependencies identified

**2. Define the Nexus Goal**:
- Overall sprint goal for all teams
- Aligns teams toward common objective
- Guides decision-making

**3. Collaborate with Teams**:
- Available to all teams for questions
- Participates in Nexus events
- Clarifies requirements across teams

**4. Stakeholder Management**:
- Gathers input from all stakeholders
- Manages expectations
- Communicates progress at Nexus level

**Challenges**:
- One PO can be stretched across many teams
- Must prioritize for whole product, not favorites
- Needs deep product knowledge

**Support**:
- NIT helps with coordination
- Teams help with refinement
- May have PO representatives (but PO retains authority)

**The PO's Time**:
- Full-time role
- Cannot be part-time with many teams
- Needs strong organizational skills

content.title: Scrum Master in Nexus
content.explanation:
In Nexus, there are multiple Scrum Masters—one per team, plus one who serves the Nexus Integration Team.

**Scrum Master Responsibilities**:

**To Their Team**:
- Standard Scrum Master duties
- Coach team on Scrum
- Remove team impediments

**To the Nexus**:
- Participate in Nexus events
- Help identify cross-team issues
- Coach team on integration
- Collaborate with other Scrum Masters

**Nexus Scrum Master**:
- One Scrum Master (often the most experienced) serves the NIT
- Facilitates Nexus events
- Coaches other Scrum Masters
- Removes systemic impediments
- Ensures Nexus process is followed

**Scrum Master Community**:
- Scrum Masters meet regularly
- Share challenges and solutions
- Improve coaching across Nexus
- Work on systemic improvements

**Scrum Master as Integrator**:
- Helps teams communicate
- Facilitates dependency resolution
- Ensures integration happens
- Not the same as technical integration lead

content.title: Nexus Integration Team Structure
content: │ NIT Member    │  │ NIT Member    │  │ NIT Member    │
│ (from Team A) │  │ (from Team B) │  │ (from Team C) │
│    SCRUM TEAM A     │ │    SCRUM TEAM B     │
KEY INSIGHT: NIT members are not a separate layer—they're
content.caption: The Nexus Integration Team connects to all Scrum Teams through its members

content.title: Nexus Integration Team in Action
content.scenario: Three teams working on e-commerce platform
content.outcome: Dependencies identified and managed early
content.details: During Nexus Daily Scrum, NIT member from Team A mentions they need an API from Team B by Thursday. Team B's NIT member confirms they can deliver, but need Team C's database changes first. Team C's NIT member says they're on track. The NIT facilitates this conversation daily, ensuring dependencies are visible and managed. Without Nexus, this would be discovered at end of sprint, causing delays.

content.question: Scenario 2: In a Nexus with 4 teams, who is accountable for ensuring the integrated increment is produced each sprint?
content.explanation: The Nexus Integration Team is explicitly accountable for the integrated increment. While teams do the integration work, the NIT ensures it happens by coordinating, coaching, and removing impediments. This is their primary responsibility.

content.title: Nexus Sprint Planning
content.explanation:
Nexus Sprint Planning is a two-part event that aligns all teams before they do their individual planning.

**Purpose**:
- Define the Nexus Goal (overall sprint goal)
- Select which Product Backlog items each team will work on
- Identify cross-team dependencies
- Create initial plan for integration

**Who Attends**:
- Product Owner
- Nexus Integration Team
- Representatives from each Scrum Team (often all team members attend)

**Duration**:
- Timeboxed, typically 2-4 hours depending on number of teams

**Agenda**:

**Part 1: Overall Alignment (60-90 min)**
1. **PO presents top of backlog**: Highest priority items, business context
2. **Teams discuss**: Which items could they take? What are the dependencies?
3. **Define Nexus Goal**: Single goal for all teams this sprint
4. **Draft team assignments**: Tentative which team takes which items
5. **Identify dependencies**: Capture on dependency board

**Part 2: Team Planning (60-90 min)**
- Each team plans their own sprint (standard Sprint Planning)
- Teams break items into tasks
- Teams create their Sprint Backlogs

**During Team Planning**:
- NIT members may float between teams to coordinate
- Dependencies are refined
- Integration plan emerges

**Outputs**:
- Nexus Goal (overall sprint goal)
- Team assignments for Product Backlog items
- Identified dependencies
- Team Sprint Backlogs
- Integration plan (how and when integration will happen)

content.title: Nexus Daily Scrum
content.explanation:
The Nexus Daily Scrum is a daily coordination event for teams to inspect progress toward the Nexus Goal and identify cross-team issues.

**Purpose**:
- Identify and manage dependencies
- Highlight integration issues
- Coordinate cross-team work
- Adjust plans across teams

**Who Attends**:
- Nexus Integration Team
- Representatives from each Scrum Team (often 1-2 people per team)

**Not Required**:
- Entire teams (they have their own Daily Scrums)
- Stakeholders

**Duration**:
- Timeboxed to 15 minutes

**Typical Agenda**:

**1. Review Nexus Goal**: Are we on track overall?

**2. Each team representative answers**:
- What did our team do yesterday that affects other teams?
- What will our team do today that affects other teams?
- What cross-team impediments do we see?

**3. Review dependency board**:
- Are any dependencies at risk?
- Any new dependencies identified?

**4. Identify actions**:
- Who needs to talk to whom after this meeting?

**What It Is NOT**:
- A status report to management
- A problem-solving session (take issues offline)
- A replacement for team Daily Scrums

**After the Meeting**:
- Representatives take information back to their teams
- Teams adjust their daily plans accordingly
- NIT coordinates follow-up on issues

content.title: Nexus Events Timeline
content.caption: Nexus events run alongside standard Scrum events throughout the sprint

content.title: Nexus Sprint Review
content.explanation:
The Nexus Sprint Review is where all teams and stakeholders inspect the integrated increment and adapt the Product Backlog.

**Purpose**:
- Demonstrate the fully integrated product
- Get feedback from stakeholders
- Review progress toward product goals
- Update Product Backlog based on learning

**Who Attends**:
- All Scrum Teams
- Nexus Integration Team
- Product Owner
- Stakeholders (customers, users, management)
- Optional: other interested parties

**Duration**:
- Timeboxed, typically 2-3 hours

**Agenda**:

**1. Welcome and Context (15 min)**
- PO presents Nexus Goal and overall progress
- Recap of what was planned

**2. Demo of Integrated Increment (60-90 min)**
- Show working, integrated software
- Not just team demos—show how features work together
- Multiple formats possible:
  - Walk through user journeys
  - Highlight key features
  - Demonstrate integration points

**3. Feedback Gathering (30 min)**
- Stakeholders ask questions
- PO captures feedback
- Discussion of what was learned

**4. Backlog Review (15 min)**
- Review timeline, budget, progress
- Discuss any changes in priorities
- Update Product Backlog based on feedback

**5. Close and Next Steps (10 min)**
- Thank stakeholders
- Preview next sprint focus

**Key Difference from Team Reviews**:
- Shows integrated product, not parts
- Stakeholders see whole picture
- Cross-team feedback

content.title: Nexus Sprint Retrospective
content.explanation:
The Nexus Retrospective focuses on the cross-team process—how teams work together and how the Nexus itself is working.

**Purpose**:
- Inspect the Nexus (cross-team) process
- Identify systemic impediments
- Create improvement experiments for the whole Nexus

**Who Attends**:
- Nexus Integration Team
- Representatives from each Scrum Team (often 2-3 per team)
- Optional: Scrum Masters from each team

**Duration**:
- Timeboxed, typically 1-2 hours

**Agenda**:

**1. Set the Stage (10 min)**
- Review agenda
- Establish safety and focus

**2. Gather Data (20 min)**
- What worked well in cross-team collaboration?
- What problems did we encounter?
- Review metrics (dependencies resolved, integration issues, etc.)

**3. Generate Insights (30 min)**
- Why did problems occur?
- Root cause analysis of systemic issues
- Identify patterns across teams

**4. Decide What to Do (20 min)**
- Choose 1-3 improvement experiments
- Define actions and owners
- Add to improvement backlog

**5. Close (10 min)**
- Review decisions
- Thank participants

**Common Themes**:
- Dependency management
- Integration frequency
- Communication across teams
- Shared technical practices
- Definition of Done alignment

**Follow-up**:
- Experiments tried in next sprint
- Progress reviewed at next Nexus Retrospective
- Systemic issues escalated to management

content.title: Nexus Artifacts
content.explanation:
Nexus adds a few artifacts to standard Scrum artifacts:

**1. Product Backlog (same as Scrum)**:
- Single backlog for whole product
- Prioritized by value
- Items clear enough for multiple teams

**2. Nexus Sprint Backlog**:
- Not a separate backlog, but a view
- Shows which teams are working on which items
- Includes identified dependencies
- Helps visualize cross-team work

**3. Integrated Increment**:
- The sum of all teams' work, integrated
- Must meet Definition of Done
- Produced at least once per sprint
- Potentially releasable

**4. Nexus Goal**:
- Overall sprint goal for all teams
- Aligns teams toward common objective
- Guides decision-making during sprint

**5. Dependency Board**:
- Visual management of dependencies
- Shows what each team needs from others
- Updated daily
- Discussed at Nexus Daily Scrum

**6. Improvement Backlog**:
- Items for improving the Nexus process
- Created in Nexus Retrospective
- Worked on alongside product work

**Transparency is Key**:
All artifacts are visible to all teams. No hidden information. Dependencies are explicit. Progress is clear.

content.title: Dependency Board in Action
content.scenario: Four teams with multiple dependencies each sprint
content.outcome: Dependencies visible and managed daily
content.prevention: No missed dependencies causing late surprises
content.details: Teams use a physical or digital dependency board. Columns: "Needed From", "What", "By When", "Status". Each dependency is a card. At Nexus Daily Scrum, teams review board. A card shows: Team B needs API from Team A by Wednesday. Status: In progress. Team A confirms they're on track. Team B notes they'll start integration Thursday. When API is delivered, card moves to "Done". Everyone sees status. No one forgets. Dependencies managed.

content.question: Scenario 3: During a Nexus Daily Scrum, Team A says they need something from Team B that wasn't planned. What should happen?
options: Ignore it—it's too late to change
Add it to dependency board, discuss impact, and adjust plans if needed
Team B must drop everything and deliver
content.explanation: The Nexus Daily Scrum is exactly for surfacing such needs. The dependency is added to the board. Teams discuss impact. Maybe Team B can deliver, maybe the scope adjusts, maybe Team A finds another way. The key is visibility and quick adaptation, not rigid planning.

content.title: Nexus Adoption Steps
content.explanation:
Adopting Nexus is a journey. Here's a typical path:

**Step 1: Ensure Scrum Mastery**
- Each team must be solid at Scrum
- If teams aren't doing Scrum well, fix that first
- Nexus amplifies good and bad practices

**Step 2: Identify the Product**
- One product with clear boundaries
- Multiple teams already working on it
- Stakeholders identified

**Step 3: Form the Nexus Integration Team**
- Appoint overall Product Owner
- Identify Scrum Master for Nexus
- Select NIT members from each team

**Step 4: Define One Definition of Done**
- Agree on single DoD across all teams
- May start with existing team DoDs and merge
- Must be achievable by all teams

**Step 5: Establish the Product Backlog**
- Merge any team backlogs into one
- Prioritize for whole product
- Refine with all teams

**Step 6: Run First Nexus Sprint**
- Conduct Nexus Sprint Planning
- Teams plan their work
- Execute with Nexus Daily Scrum
- Integrate frequently
- Nexus Sprint Review and Retrospective

**Step 7: Inspect and Adapt**
- Learn from first sprint
- Adjust process
- Improve technical practices
- Expand to more teams if needed

**Common First Sprint Challenges**:
- Dependencies not fully identified
- Integration takes longer than expected
- Definition of Done too loose or too tight
- Communication overhead feels high

**Expectations**:
- First few sprints may be slower
- Learning curve is real
- Improvement comes with practice

content.title: Technical Practices for Nexus
content.explanation:
Nexus, like LeSS, requires strong technical practices to succeed.

**Why Technical Practices Matter**:
- Multiple teams modify same codebase
- Integration must happen frequently
- Without automation, integration becomes bottleneck
- Quality must be built in, not inspected after

**Essential Technical Practices**:

**Continuous Integration (CI)**:
- All code integrated at least daily
- Automated build and test
- Fast feedback on integration issues

**Automated Testing**:
- Unit tests (fast, many)
- Integration tests (verify component interaction)
- Acceptance tests (verify features)
- Run in CI pipeline

**Test-Driven Development (TDD)**:
- Tests before code
- Clean, testable design
- Regression safety

**Continuous Delivery/Deployment**:
- Ability to release anytime
- Automated deployment pipelines
- Low-risk releases

**Feature Toggles**:
- Hide incomplete features
- Enable trunk-based development
- Decouple deployment from release

**Component Architecture**:
- Clear boundaries between components
- Well-defined interfaces
- Teams can work independently

**Collective Code Ownership**:
- Any team can change any code
- Shared coding standards
- Code reviews across teams

**The Integration Challenge**:
Without these practices, integration becomes a separate phase. Teams work in isolation, then spend days integrating at the end. This defeats the purpose of Nexus.

**Invest Early**:
Make technical excellence a priority from day one. Dedicate time to improve automation, refactor code, and train teams.

content.title: Nexus Integration Flow
content.caption: Continuous Integration is essential for Nexus to work effectively

content.title: Nexus and Distributed Teams
content.explanation:
Nexus can work with distributed teams, but it requires deliberate practices.

**Challenges**:
- Time zone differences
- Communication barriers
- Integration harder
- Dependency visibility reduced

**Practices for Distributed Nexus**:

**1. Overlap Hours**:
- Establish core hours when all teams overlap
- Schedule Nexus Daily Scrum during overlap
- Ensure NIT members available

**2. Virtual Dependency Board**:
- Digital tool for dependency tracking
- Updated in real-time
- Visible to all teams

**3. Frequent Synchronization**:
- Nexus Daily Scrum without fail
- Additional cross-team syncs as needed
- Video on for all meetings

**4. Strong CI/CD**:
- Even more important when distributed
- Automated integration across sites
- No manual integration steps

**5. Periodic Co-location**:
- If possible, bring teams together for PI Planning or major events
- Build relationships across sites
- Overcome 'us vs. them' mentality

**6. Clear Communication Protocols**:
- Which tools for which purposes
- Response time expectations
- Escalation paths

**7. Invest in Tools**:
- Good video conferencing
- Collaborative documentation
- Integrated development environments

**Distributed Nexus Can Work**:
Many organizations run Nexus successfully with distributed teams. It requires more discipline, but the framework itself doesn't require co-location.

content.title: Distributed Nexus Success
content.scenario: Company with teams in US, Europe, and India
content.outcome: Successful Nexus implementation across 12 time zones
content.details: Teams in 3 countries, 12 time zones apart. Core overlap hours 8-11am US Eastern (afternoon Europe, evening India). Nexus Daily Scrum at 9am ET. Dependency board in Jira, updated continuously. Strong CI pipeline integrates code from all locations within 30 minutes of commit. Quarterly, all team leads meet in person for relationship building. After initial challenges, Nexus now runs smoothly. Key success factors: disciplined communication, automation, and leadership commitment to distributed work.

content.question: Scenario 4: A Nexus implementation with distributed teams is struggling with integration. Code from different locations doesn't work together. What's the most likely root cause?
options: Insufficient CI/CD automation—integration should be automated, not manual
content.explanation: Integration problems across distributed teams usually indicate insufficient CI/CD automation. When integration is manual or infrequent, code diverges. The solution is to invest in automated build, test, and integration pipelines that catch issues quickly, not more meetings.

content.title: Nexus Resources and Community
content.explanation:
Resources for learning more about Nexus:

**Official Sources**:
- **Scrum.org**: Home of Nexus, free resources, case studies
- **Nexus Guide**: Official framework description (free PDF)
- **Nexus Training**: Professional Scrum with Nexus course

**Books**:
- "The Nexus Framework for Scaling Scrum" by Kurt Bittner and Patricia Kong
- "Scaling Professional Scrum with Nexus" (upcoming)

**Community**:
- Scrum.org discussion forums
- Local Scrum user groups
- Nexus practitioners community

**Certifications**:
- Professional Scrum with Nexus (PSN) certification
- For Scrum Masters, Product Owners, team members
- Demonstrates understanding of Nexus

**Case Studies**:
- Available on Scrum.org website
- Real-world implementations
- Lessons learned

**Getting Started**:
- Read the Nexus Guide (30 minutes)
- Take an online course
- Try with 3 teams in a simulation
- Experiment, learn, adapt

**The Nexus Community**:
Join others scaling Scrum. Share challenges and solutions. Learn from experienced practitioners.

content.value:
Remember: Nexus is Scrum with just enough structure to handle multiple teams. It doesn't invent new complexity—it reveals and manages the complexity that already exists in cross-team work.

The goal isn't to 'do Nexus.' The goal is to deliver a valuable, integrated product increment every sprint using multiple teams. Nexus is just a means to that end.

Start with strong Scrum teams. Add Nexus when you need coordination. Keep technical practices excellent. Inspect and adapt continuously. And never forget that at the heart of Nexus are people building great software together.

tutorials.title: 🎵 Spotify Model - Culture, Autonomy, and Alignment at Scale
tutorials.description: Master the Spotify Model for organizing Agile teams at scale. Learn how Squads, Tribes, Chapters, and Guilds create a culture of autonomy, alignment, and continuous learning.

content.title: The Heart of the Spotify Model - Culture Over Framework
What is the Spotify Model?
content.explanation:
The Spotify Model is not a framework—it's a people-driven, autonomous approach to scaling Agile that Spotify developed and shared with the world. It's based on the idea that culture, not process, is what enables agility at scale.

**Origin Story**:
In 2012, Spotify engineers Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson published a paper describing how Spotify organized its engineering teams. They didn't intend to create a 'model'—they just shared what worked for them. But the ideas resonated globally, and the 'Spotify Model' was born.

**Key Philosophy**:
- **Culture eats process for breakfast**
- **Autonomy with alignment**—teams decide how, but align on why
- **Organic growth** over rigid structure
- **Continuous learning** through communities

**Important Caveat**:
Spotify itself has evolved and doesn't follow this model exactly anymore. It was a snapshot in time, not a prescription. The value is in the principles, not the specific structure.

**The Spotify Model is NOT**:
- A framework to implement (like SAFe or LeSS)
- One-size-fits-all
- Static—it evolves
- A replacement for Scrum or Kanban

**Key Insight**: The Spotify Model is about creating an environment where Agile teams thrive—autonomous, aligned, and constantly learning.

content.title: Spotify Model Structure Overview
content: │ • GUILD: Community of interest across tribes                    │
│ • CHAPTER LEAD: Line manager, skill coach                      │
content.caption: The Spotify Model organizes teams into squads, tribes, chapters, and guilds

content.title: Core Principles of the Spotify Model
content.explanation:
The Spotify Model is built on several key principles that matter more than the structure:

**1. Autonomy with Alignment**
- Squads are autonomous—they decide what to build and how
- But they align on the overall mission and strategy
- 'Mission command'—leaders define 'why', teams figure out 'how'

**2. Culture of Learning**
- Failure is learning, not blame
- Experiments over big design up front
- Sharing knowledge across teams (chapters, guilds)

**3. Minimize Handoffs**
- Squads are cross-functional (dev, test, UX, etc.)
- End-to-end ownership
- Reduce dependencies between teams

**4. Loose Coupling, High Cohesion**
- Teams loosely coupled (can work independently)
- Within team, high cohesion (everything needed)
- Architecture supports this (microservices, APIs)

**5. Organic Growth**
- Structure follows need, not top-down design
- Squads form around mission
- Evolve over time

**6. Leadership as Coaching**
- Leaders enable, not control
- Remove impediments
- Grow people

**7. Continuous Improvement**
- Retrospectives at all levels
- Experiment with new ways of working
- Share learnings across organization

**Key Insight**: These principles are more important than the specific names (squad, tribe, etc.). Apply the principles in your context.

content.title: Spotify Model Structures at a Glance
Spotify Model vs. Other Scaling Approaches
content.explanation:
How the Spotify Model compares to other scaling frameworks:

| Aspect | Spotify Model | SAFe | LeSS | Nexus |
|--------|--------------|------|------|-------|
| **Origin** | Spotify's culture | Scaled Agile, Inc. | Larman & Vodde | Scrum.org |
| **Philosophy** | Culture-driven | Comprehensive | Minimalist | Minimalist |
| **Structure** | Organic, evolving | Prescribed | Prescribed | Prescribed |
| **Roles** | Few, flexible | Many | Few | Few + NIT |
| **Team type** | Cross-functional | Cross-functional | Feature teams | Scrum teams |
| **Coordination** | Informal, communities | PI Planning, ART | Overall events | Nexus events |
| **Best for** | Product orgs with strong culture | Enterprise transformation | Pure Scrum scaling | Scrum teams needing integration |

**Key Difference**:
The Spotify Model is less prescriptive. It describes a way of organizing, not a step-by-step process. It's about creating the right culture and letting practices emerge.

**Can You Combine Them?**:
Yes. Many organizations use Spotify's squad/tribe structure with SAFe's PI Planning, or LeSS's feature teams with Spotify's guilds. The structures are complementary.

content.question: Scenario 1: A company wants to adopt the Spotify Model. They download the diagrams and start renaming their teams to Squads, Tribes, Chapters, and Guilds. What's the problem?
options: Nothing—that's exactly how you adopt it
They're missing the point—the model is about culture and principles, not just renaming
They need to hire Spotify coaches
They should start with SAFe instead
content.explanation: This is the most common mistake. The Spotify Model isn't a renaming exercise. It's about creating a culture of autonomy, alignment, and learning. If you just change names without changing how you work, you'll get nothing but confusion.

items.myth: The Spotify Model is a framework like SAFe
items.reality: It's a cultural model, not a prescriptive framework

items.myth: Spotify still uses this model today
items.reality: They've evolved; it was a snapshot in time

items.myth: You need Spotify-sized teams to use it
items.reality: The principles apply at any scale

items.myth: Chapters and guilds are mandatory
items.reality: They're examples; create what works for you

items.myth: The Spotify Model replaces Scrum
items.reality: Squads often use Scrum; it's complementary

content.title: The Building Blocks: Squads, Tribes, Chapters, Guilds
Squad - The Autonomous Team
content.explanation:
The squad is the fundamental building block of the Spotify Model—a cross-functional, autonomous team that owns a feature area end-to-end.

**Squad Characteristics**:

**Size**: 6-12 people (like a Scrum team)

**Composition**:
- Developers
- Tester
- UX Designer
- Product Owner
- (Sometimes other specialists)

**Autonomy**:
- Squad decides what to build and how
- Has all skills needed to deliver value
- Can deploy independently (with appropriate architecture)

**Mission**:
- Long-lived mission (e.g., "Playback", "Search", "Monetization")
- Not project-based—stays together
- Owns their part of the product long-term

**Accountability**:
- Responsible for their features
- Responsible for quality
- Responsible for their own way of working

**Alignment**:
- Aligns with tribe mission
- Participates in tribe-level planning
- Coordinates with other squads as needed

**Squad Practices**:
- Most squads use Scrum or Kanban
- Regular retrospectives
- Continuous improvement
- End-to-end ownership

**Squad Analogy**:
Think of a squad as a mini-startup within the company. They have their own mission, their own skills, and the freedom to figure out how to achieve it.

content.title: Squad Structure
content: │ • Cross-functional: all skills needed to deliver value          │
│ • Autonomous: decides what to build and how                     │
│ • End-to-end responsible: from idea to production               │
│ • Aligned with tribe and company mission                        │
content.caption: A squad is a mini-startup with end-to-end responsibility for its mission

content.title: Tribe - The Squad Family
content.explanation:
A tribe is a collection of squads that work in related areas. Think of it as an incubator for squads.

**Tribe Characteristics**:

**Size**: 40-150 people (typically 4-12 squads)

**Purpose**:
- Provide a supportive environment for squads
- Facilitate coordination between squads
- Share resources and knowledge
- Maintain overall direction

**Tribe Lead**:
- Responsible for the tribe's overall health
- Coaches squad product owners
- Removes impediments at tribe level
- Not a traditional manager—more of a coach and coordinator

**Tribe Boundaries**:
- Tribes are organized around broad product areas
- Example: "Playback Tribe", "Discovery Tribe", "Monetization Tribe"
- Boundaries should minimize dependencies between tribes

**Tribe Practices**:

**Tribe Sync**: Regular meeting of squad representatives to coordinate

**Tribe Retrospective**: Squads reflect on cross-squad issues

**Tribe Demo**: Show what the whole tribe has accomplished

**Tribe Planning**: Align on priorities for upcoming period

**Tribe Culture**:
- Each tribe develops its own culture within company norms
- Physical colocation (when possible) in tribe area
- Shared space for collaboration

**Tribe Dependency Management**:
- Tribes should be loosely coupled
- APIs and contracts between tribes
- Minimize need for cross-tribe coordination

**Tribe Analogy**: Think of a tribe as a small company focused on a product area, with squads as its teams.

content.title: Chapter - The Skill Family
content.explanation:
A chapter is a family of people with similar skills within a tribe. Chapters solve the 'how do people grow' problem in autonomous squad structures.

**Why Chapters Exist**:
In autonomous squads, people with the same skill (e.g., frontend developers) are spread across squads. They need a way to:
- Share knowledge
- Maintain standards
- Grow in their craft
- Have career conversations

**Chapter Characteristics**:

**Composition**:
- People with the same skill/role across squads in a tribe
- Example: "Frontend Chapter", "QA Chapter", "UX Chapter"

**Size**: Typically 5-10 people (can be larger)

**Chapter Lead**:
- Usually an experienced person in that skill
- Acts as line manager for chapter members
- Coaches on technical practices
- Conducts performance reviews
- Not a project manager—doesn't assign work

**Chapter Activities**:

**Regular Meetings**:
- Share learnings from squads
- Discuss technical challenges
- Develop coding standards

**Skill Development**:
- Training and workshops
- Mentoring junior members
- Career path discussions

**Cross-Pollination**:
- Spread good practices across squads
- Identify common problems
- Suggest improvements

**Chapter vs. Squad**:
- Squad is where you work (the mission)
- Chapter is where you grow (the craft)
- You belong to one squad, one chapter

**Chapter Analogy**: Think of a chapter as a guild within the tribe—a community of practice with managerial responsibilities.

content: │  │   SQUAD A   │  │   SQUAD B   │  │   SQUAD C   │             │
│  │ • Dev A1    │  │ • Dev B1    │  │ • Dev C1    │◄──┐         │
│  │ • Dev A2    │  │ • Dev B2    │  │ • Dev C2    │   │         │
